message.content:
{
  "frontend": {
    "needed": true,
    "prompt": "Explicit contract facts (repeat):
- Superuser may read other users' entries (GET of another user's resource must be allowed and return 200).
- PUT and DELETE of another user's resource must return HTTP 403 with JSON body exactly {"detail": "Read-only access"}.
- The frontend must render other users' entries as read-only (no edit UI, no delete UI, no inline editable fields).
- Superuser may write (PUT/DELETE) his/her own entries (owner == current user) — writes on own resources must be allowed.
- Normal (non-superuser) users attempting to access other users' resources must get HTTP 404 (the backend must hide existence from non-owners).
- A request for a non-existent resource must result in HTTP 404.
- On create (POST), the resource owner_id must be set by the backend to the current authenticated user; the frontend must NOT supply or override owner_id in the POST payload.

Front-end implementation instructions (scope decided from the requirement):
1) UI behavior and state
   - When rendering a resource details page or resource list item, show editing controls (edit button, delete button, inline editable fields) only when the resource is known to be editable by the current user (see ownership/editable detection below). Otherwise show the resource in read-only mode.
   - Do not send owner_id in POST create requests. Never allow the user to change owner_id in the client UI.

2) How to determine editability (must coordinate on one of these; if not negotiated, implement safe default):
   - Preferred contract to implement now: use the resource.owner_id returned by the backend and compare it to the client-known currentUserId. If owner_id === currentUserId, enable full edit/delete; otherwise read-only. If the backend additionally returns a boolean resource.editable, that may be used instead of or in addition to the owner_id check; treat resource.editable === true as editable.
   - Important omission to note (requires backend agreement): the requirement does not specify how the frontend obtains the current user's id (currentUserId) or whether the backend will include owner_id or an editable flag in responses. Do NOT assume these are present. Before final implementation, confirm with backend one of:
     a) The API responses include owner_id in the resource representation and the application exposes currentUserId in the client session/token; OR
     b) The API responses include an explicit editable boolean (resource.editable) for the requesting user.
   - Safe fallback if coordination is not completed: render resource read-only (disable edit/delete) and show an explanatory non-technical message like "Editing disabled until ownership is verified".

3) HTTP response handling and UX flows
   - GET resource/:id
     • On 200: show resource. Decide editability per step 2.
     • On 404: show Not Found UI (same treatment for non-existent resource and for normal-user requesting another user's resource).
     • Do not assume GET will return 403 based on the requirement; if GET returns 403, handle it by showing read-only UI and surface the server message; log for backend coordination.
   - PUT resource/:id (attempt to save edits)
     • On 200 (or 204 with subsequent GET): consider save successful and refresh UI.
     • On 403 with JSON {"detail": "Read-only access"}: show a clear error message: "Cannot modify this resource — read-only access." Remove or disable edit controls for this resource thereafter.
     • On 404: show Not Found (resource absent / access denied). Treat as if resource no longer exists.
   - DELETE resource/:id
     • On 204/200: consider delete successful and remove resource from UI.
     • On 403 with JSON {"detail": "Read-only access"}: show error "Cannot delete this resource — read-only access." Do not expose a retry-edit path.
     • On 404: show Not Found.
   - POST create
     • Do not include owner_id in POST body. On 201 success, use returned resource from backend to render created item. If backend returns owner_id, use it to update UI/editability.

4) Error handling and UX details
   - For 403 responses, specifically check that body.detail === "Read-only access" and display the exact human message derived from it. Log the event for diagnostics.
   - For 404 responses, do not reveal additional details; present a generic Not Found page/modal.

5) Tests and acceptance checks the frontend must include
   - As a superuser: GET another user's resource returns 200 and UI shows read-only; attempts to PUT/DELETE the other user's resource result in 403 with the specified JSON and the UI displays the Read-only message.
   - As a superuser on own resource: PUT/DELETE succeed.
   - As a normal user: GET of another user's resource results in 404 and UI shows Not Found.
   - For non-existent resource id: GET, PUT, DELETE result in 404 and UI shows Not Found.
   - On create: POST without owner_id; verify returned resource.owner_id (if present) equals current user.

6) Implementation notes and explicit omissions (do not guess):
   - The requirement does NOT specify exact API endpoint URLs, request/response schemas beyond owner_id and error JSON, nor how the client obtains currentUserId or authentication tokens. Do NOT assume header names, path patterns, or authentication details. Coordinate with backend to confirm:
     • The exact resource endpoints (e.g., /resources/:id) and HTTP status codes for success responses (200 vs 204 for PUT/DELETE).
     • Whether resource responses include owner_id and/or an editable boolean.
     • How the client exposes currentUserId (session, token, separate /me endpoint).
   - Until those are agreed, implement UI defensively (default to read-only if ownership cannot be determined).

Deliverables for frontend implementer:
- UI changes to hide/disable edit/delete controls for non-editable resources.
- Network-layer handlers for GET/PUT/DELETE/POST that implement the response handling above (403 JSON parsing, 404 as Not Found).
- Automated tests that assert the acceptance checks listed in section 5.

Do not invent or assume any authentication header names, token contents, or backend data shape beyond the explicit facts above. Coordinate with backend on the unresolved items listed."
  },
  "backend": {
    "needed": true,
    "prompt": "Explicit contract facts (repeat):
- Superuser may read other users' entries (GET of another user's resource must be allowed and return 200).
- PUT and DELETE of another user's resource must return HTTP 403 with JSON body exactly {"detail": "Read-only access"}.
- The frontend must render other users' entries as read-only (frontend requirement; backend must supply responses to allow this behavior).
- Superuser may write (PUT/DELETE) his/her own entries (owner == current user) — writes on own resources must be allowed.
- Normal (non-superuser) users attempting to access other users' resources must get HTTP 404 (the backend must hide existence from non-owners).
- A request for a non-existent resource must result in HTTP 404.
- On create (POST), the resource owner_id must be set by the backend to the current authenticated user; the frontend must NOT supply or override owner_id in the POST payload.

Back-end implementation instructions (scope decided from the requirement):
1) Authentication and identity (required scope decision):
   - Access control must be evaluated based on the authenticated requestor: the backend must use the server's authentication context to obtain the current user's unique id (current_user_id) and a boolean is_superuser flag for the request. The requirement does not prescribe a specific authentication mechanism; use the application's existing auth middleware to obtain these values.
   - Explicit note (omission): the requirement does not name header formats or token schemes. Do NOT invent new auth semantics; use the system's established auth context values.

2) Resource representation contract (required to enable frontend behavior):
   - Include owner_id in the resource JSON representation returned by GET and POST responses. This allows the frontend to determine ownership. (This follows the requirement that owner_id exists and must be set on create.)
   - Optionally you may also include a computed boolean editable for convenience, but do not remove owner_id. If you add editable, it must reflect the same ACL rules described below.

3) Endpoint access control rules (must be implemented exactly):
   - GET /resources/:id
     • If resource does not exist: respond 404.
     • If requestor is resource.owner: respond 200 with resource JSON (include owner_id).
     • If requestor is superuser and requestor != owner: respond 200 with resource JSON (include owner_id).
     • If requestor is not owner and not superuser: respond 404 (hide existence).
   - PUT /resources/:id (update)
     • If resource does not exist: respond 404.
     • If requestor is resource.owner: accept update, persist changes, respond with appropriate success (200 with updated resource or 204 and no content) — be consistent with your API conventions.
     • If requestor is superuser and requestor != owner: do NOT permit update; respond 403 with JSON exactly {"detail": "Read-only access"}.
     • If requestor is not owner and not superuser: respond 404.
   - DELETE /resources/:id
     • If resource does not exist: respond 404.
     • If requestor is resource.owner: delete resource and respond with appropriate success (204 or 200) consistent with API conventions.
     • If requestor is superuser and requestor != owner: do NOT permit delete; respond 403 with JSON exactly {"detail": "Read-only access"}.
     • If requestor is not owner and not superuser: respond 404.
   - POST /resources
     • Create a new resource. Ignore any owner_id supplied in the client payload; set owner_id = current_user_id from the authenticated requestor context. Return 201 Created with the created resource representation (include owner_id).

4) Error body and status exactness (must match frontend expectations):
   - The 403 response for attempts by a superuser to modify another user's resource MUST be JSON with a top-level field detail whose string value is exactly "Read-only access".
   - 404 responses for non-existence or unauthorized discovery suppression must not expose additional ownership metadata.

5) Tests and acceptance checks backend must provide
   - As a superuser, GET another user's resource returns 200.
   - As a superuser, PUT/DELETE another user's resource return 403 with exact JSON {"detail": "Read-only access"}.
   - As a superuser, PUT/DELETE on their own resource succeed.
   - As a normal user, GET of another user's resource returns 404.
   - For a non-existent resource id, GET/PUT/DELETE return 404.
   - POST create sets owner_id equal to the authenticated creating user regardless of any owner_id in the request body.
   - The JSON returned for resources includes owner_id so the frontend can determine editability.

6) Implementation notes and explicit omissions (do not guess):
   - The requirement does not prescribe exact URL paths, resource field names beyond owner_id, or the precise success status codes for PUT/DELETE (200 vs 204). Choose consistent conventions for your API but document them and share with frontend. Do NOT assume the frontend already knows them.
   - The requirement does not prescribe the authentication transport. Use the existing authentication middleware/context to supply current_user_id and is_superuser to ACL checks. Document which values are consumed (e.g., request.user.id and request.user.is_superuser) so the frontend and contractors understand how owner_id and user identity map.

Deliverables for backend implementer:
- Server-side ACL enforcement implementing the exact rules above, with tests covering all acceptance cases.
- Resource JSON responses including owner_id (and optional editable boolean if desired), and exact 403 error body for disallowed superuser modifications.
- Documentation of the API endpoints, expected request/response schemas, and how current_user_id and is_superuser are derived from the auth system so the frontend can implement ownership checks.

Do not invent or assume any client-side session format or header names. Confirm the exact endpoint paths, response payload field names, and auth-context variable names with the frontend before final integration."
  }
}
